analysis.investment_thesis: Clean Science is an admirable business — zero debt, 27% net profit CAGR over seven years, and exceptional returns on capital — but Mr. Market is pricing it at INR 757 against a Graham Number of roughly INR 271, a 2.8x premium that leaves no margin of safety whatsoever. At P/E 32.8x and P/B 5.36x I am paying for a story of future growth, not for proven earning power at a discount.
key_strengths: Virtually zero debt (borrowings INR 2 Cr against equity of INR 1,500 Cr) — fortress balance sheet by any standard
Consistent and growing profitability: net profit expanded from INR 49 Cr (2018) to INR 264 Cr (2025), positive every single year
Outstanding ROCE of 27.3% and operating margin of 24% — genuinely rare for a commodity-adjacent chemicals business
key_risks: P/E of 32.8x demands continued high growth; any revenue deceleration (2024 showed a dip to INR 791 Cr from INR 936 Cr) will collapse the valuation
Free cash flow has been erratic (negative in FY22, only INR 10 Cr in FY24) due to heavy capex; CWIP doubled to INR 98 Cr, returns on new capacity unproven
Single-product concentration in specialty antioxidants (MEHQ, BHA, TBHQ) makes earnings vulnerable to pricing or regulatory shocks in any key application segment
red_flags: Price of INR 757 is 2.8x the Graham Number of ~INR 271 (using EPS ~INR 23, BVPS ~INR 141)
P/B of 5.36 — paying INR 5.36 for every rupee of book value, a speculative premium by my standards
Revenue fell 15% in FY24 before recovering in FY25 — growth is not as steady as the CAGR implies
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Clean Science passes every balance-sheet test I require: no debt, strong reserves, positive operating cash flow in all five recent years, and growing retained earnings. Its operating margin of 24% and ROCE of 27% are the hallmarks of a genuine moat built on catalytic process chemistry. However, the intelligent investor must separate business quality from price paid, and here the price fails completely — the stock trades at 32.8x earnings and 5.4x book, embedding years of optimistic growth into the current quotation.

Applying my Graham Number formula (√(22.5 × EPS × BVPS) = √(22.5 × 23 × 141) ≈ INR 271), the current price of INR 757 represents a 179% premium to intrinsic value as I calculate it. The inconsistent free cash flow despite strong reported profits — capex consumed INR 232 Cr in FY24 against operating CF of INR 236 Cr — suggests that maintaining the business requires substantial reinvestment. An excellent enterprise at a ruinous price is still a ruinous purchase.
